title: A spatiotemporal ecological–epidemiological model for malaria-borne mosquito control
short_title: Larvivorous fish against malaria: fixed versus adaptive release plans

abstract: Malaria remains one of the world's most persistent infectious diseases, driven by complex interactions among human mobility, vector ecology, and environmental heterogeneity. Because mosquito larvae concentrate in aquatic habitats, biological control using larvivorous fish has long been used as a sustainable complement to insecticides. However, introducing predatory fish creates a central ecological trade-off where the same intervention that suppresses mosquito emergence also disrupts native aquatic communities. Addressing this concern, we develop a spatiotemporal eco-epidemiological framework that links vector-borne human pandemic spread, mosquito population movement and reproduction dynamics, and two interacting fish populations in which one intervention fish is introduced to consume larvae, and a native fish population is to be conserved. Within this framework, we compare a one-time offline deployment strategy with a dynamic monitoring strategy that updates fish release in response to local system states. Our results identify conditions under which adaptive deployment achieves a better balance between reducing human infections and preserving native fish, offering a principled basis for ecologically informed malaria control in heterogeneous urban landscapes. Quantitatively, both the offline and the monitoring strategy avert roughly two-thirds of the no-intervention infection burden and differ only modestly in epidemiological outcome. The monitoring strategy attains comparable infection control at a lower native-fish loss.

summary: Fish that eat mosquito larvae can cut malaria transmission, but introduced fish also compete with native fish. We built a model that couples malaria in humans, the movement and breeding of mosquitoes, and two fish populations, written both as partial differential equations and as an agent-based simulation of a landscape reconstructed from the Panama Canal Zone around Gamboa. In it we compared a fish-release plan fixed in advance (found with Bayesian optimization) with a policy that adapts releases to monitored conditions (learned with Double DQN reinforcement learning). Both averted about two thirds of the infections expected without intervention: the fixed plan prevented slightly more infections, while the adaptive policy usually did less harm to native fish.
key_findings: Across repeated stochastic runs, the fixed offline policy averted 69.5% of the no-intervention infection burden on average and the monitoring policy 66.4%; the offline outcomes were also more tightly clustered.
Over 500 parameter sets sampled jointly with Latin hypercube sampling, both policies always reduced the infection burden, with median reductions of 72.0% (offline) and 64.2% (monitoring).
The trade-off held almost everywhere: the offline policy had the lower infection burden in all 500 parameter sets, and the monitoring policy had the lower ecological cost in 497 of 500.

Infection was concentrated near water, with about 44% of the cumulative burden within about 450 m of water and about 80% within about 1 km; fish releases lowered the burden without changing this spatial profile.

In the Morris screening, the infection burden was most sensitive to the mortality of questing mosquitoes, the predation rate of the introduced fish and larval recruitment, while the ecological cost was driven mainly by the competitive effect of the introduced fish on native fish and the native-fish growth rate.
The landscape is a stylized reconstruction of the historical Canal Zone and several ecological parameters are model assumptions, so the results are scenario analyses rather than forecasts.
